new_statements.translation: [p.13] acute accent (takiyíd / 'pahilís'): mark of stress in speech, i.e. 'stress'. ... [p.17] Minimal pairs for stress: yusóng [ju.ˈsoŋ] 'mortar' vs yúsong [ˈju.soŋ] 'lúsong'; bugsók [bug.ˈsok] 'erecting a house-post' vs búgsok [ˈbug.sok] 'person (Ata term for a fellow native)'. ... [p.43] Inata uses three accent marks: acute, grave and circumflex. The accent marks represent stress and the glottal stop. 8.1 The acute is placed over the vowel of the stressed syllable that has no accompanying glottal stop. It is used for words pronounced malumay [penultimate stress] e.g. maáju 'good', garányon 'big'; it is also used for words pronounced mabilis [final stress] e.g. sapót 'clothing', kansiyón 'song'. [8.2-8.3, p.43-45: grave = final glottal stop without stress on that syllable (malumi, e.g. aniyà 'bee', tubò 'a mushroom'); circumflex = final syllable both stressed and glottal-final (maragsa, e.g. bitû 'small', sapâ 'river', amâ 'father', inâ 'mother').]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (diin) is contrastive in Inata: it falls on either the penultimate or the final syllable as a lexical property, independent of a word-final glottal stop, giving the four Philippine-style classes malumay (penult stress, no final glottal: maáju, garányon), mabilis (final stress: sapót, kansiyón), malumi (penult stress + final glottal: aniyà, tubò) and maragsa (final stress + final glottal: bitû, sapâ, amâ, inâ); stress alone distinguishes words (yusóng vs yúsong, bugsók vs búgsok), and the orthography marks the stressed vowel with an acute (circumflex when the stressed final syllable also ends in a glottal stop).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; only penult and final stress positions are exemplified (no antepenult examples); the syllabification chapter says it is based on spelling not phonemes
new_statements.identity_note: Inata, the heritage language of the Ata (Negrito) of northern Negros Occidental (Sitio Manara, Cadiz; also Sagay, Calatrava, Toboso, Salvador Benedicto). ISO atm / ataa1240 is the only code for the Negros Ata language; Lobel 2013 notes 'possibly 2 dialects' (N Negros vs Mabinay/Bais, S-central Negros, where the SIL 1973 list and Glottolog's map point sit). This work therefore describes the northern variety. Sample Inata text shows a distinct lect (e.g. hinambayan 'language', poluy-anon 'community', regular l>y: yusong = lusong, suyat = sulat), not Hiligaynon/Cebuano. Not Ata Manobo [atd], Atta (Luzon) or Ati/Inati [atk].
